title.en: Cattle of every age; life and the breaths made fit by the sacrifice

summary: The tenth anuvāka has two halves. The first carries the refrain ca me through the herd: the unborn young and the calves, then bulls and cows by age, which Sāyaṇa makes a year and a half, two, two and a half, three, three and a half and four years old, then the breeding bull and the barren cow, the older bull and the cow that miscarries, the draught ox and the newly calved cow. The second states the verb that Sāyaṇa supplies to every item of the Chamakam: ‘may life be made fit by the sacrifice’, said of the breaths, the eye and ear, mind and speech, the self (Sāyaṇa: the body) and the sacrifice itself. Sāyaṇa reads kalpatām as ‘may it become able to do its work’.

‘bearing the second [year]’: a two-year-old (ditya probably = dvitīya, ‘second’, MW)

vyakarana.note: Nominative plural, as is vatsāḥ: the whole class is asked for. Every item of the Chamakam is a nominative subject of the supplied kalpatām.

i-stem tryavi, feminine tryavī in -ī. The second member is avi, ‘sheep’; MW renders the compound ‘three sheep-times old’, a calf of eighteen months. Sāyaṇa's ages (tryavi a year and a half, pañcāvi two and a half) imply that one avi is half a year.
Nominative singular of the stem dityavāh (MW: strong stem -vāh, nom. -vāṭ, instr. dityauhā). Final h becomes ḍh at the end of a word (P. 8.2.31), ṭ in pause.
Feminine of dityavāh in -ī. Before the vowel of the ending vāh contracts to ūh (P. 6.4.132, cited by MW), and a + ū gives au: ditya + ūhī → dityauhī.

translation.literal: Embryos and for me, calves and for me, the [male] of three avis and for me, the [female] of three avis and for me, the two-year-old [male] and for me, the two-year-old [female] and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May the unborn young be mine, and the calves; the bull and the heifer of a year and a half, and the bull and the heifer of two years.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa calls the unborn young and the calves well known («गर्भा वत्साश्च प्रसिद्धाः») and then gives each of the following terms an age. The tryavi is a young bull of a year and a half, still calf-like (वत्सरूपः); the printed bhāṣya is corrupt at this point (सार्धसंमत्सरो … पुंगवख्यविः), but the age and the bull are clear. A cow of that kind is tryavī: «तथाविधा गौस्त्र्यवी». The dityavāh is a bull of two years, «द्विसंवत्सर ऋषभो दित्यवाट्», and the dityauhī the cow of that age («तथाविधा गौर्दित्यौही»).
units.reflection: The list of cattle begins before birth, with the unborn young, and moves through the herd half a year at a time: what is asked for is a herd that continues.

flags.note: The unit of age in tryavi (and pañcāvi in unit 2) is not explained by Sāyaṇa; MW gives ‘three sheep-times old’, a calf of eighteen months. That one avi is half a year is an inference from the ages Sāyaṇa states, not something he says.
The first member of dityavāh is taken by MW, with ‘prob.’, as ditya = dvitīya, ‘second’. Sāyaṇa states only the age (two years).

translation.literal: The [male] of five avis and for me, the [female] of five avis and for me, the three-year-old [male] and for me, the three-year-old [female] and for me, the turyavāh [male] and for me, the turyauhī [female] and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May the bull and the heifer of two and a half years be mine, the bull and the heifer of three years, and the bull and the heifer of three and a half.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa continues the ages half a year at a time. The pañcāvi is a bull of two and a half years (सार्धद्विसंवत्सर), and the cow of that age is pañcāvī («गौः पञ्चावी»). The trivatsa is a bull of three years, «संवत्सरत्रयोपेत ऋषभस्त्रिवत्सः», and trivatsā the cow of that age («तथाविधा गौस्त्रिवत्सा»). The turyavāh is a bull of three and a half years, «सार्धत्रिवत्सर ऋषभस्तुर्यवाट्», and turyauhī the cow of that age.

flags.note: MW makes turyavāh / turyauhī an ox or cow four years old (turya, ‘fourth’); Sāyaṇa makes them three and a half, which keeps his series in half-years (1½, 2, 2½, 3, 3½, 4) and leaves four years for paṣṭhavāh in unit 3. The readable translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

sandhi.rule: final t before c becomes c (stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ, P. 8.4.40). The Taittirīya nominative of paṣṭhavāh ends in t (MW: nom. -vāṭ in the VS, -vāt in the TS), so the text has paṣṭhavāc ca, where dityavāṭ and turyavāṭ keep ṭ before ca
final e before a vowel becomes ay (P. 6.1.78), and the y is dropped (P. 8.3.19): me ukṣā → ma ukṣā

sandhi.type: vowel sandhi (ayādi, y dropped); visarga sandhi
sandhi.rule: me before ṛ becomes ma, as before u; ṛṣabhaḥ ca → ṛṣabhaś ca
final t before c becomes c (P. 8.4.40)

after word-final e an initial a is absorbed (eṅaḥ padāntād ati, P. 6.1.109), marked by the avagraha; final n before c is written as the palatal nasal ñ (P. 8.4.40). The Taittirīya text has no inserted sibilant here, where classical usage writes anaḍvāṃś ca (P. 8.3.7)

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi; vowel sandhi (ayādi, y dropped)
sandhi.rule: dhenuḥ ca → dhenuś ca; the last me stands before āyuḥ, the first word of unit 4, and becomes ma

samasa.meaning: ‘paṣṭha-bearer’; the sense of paṣṭha is uncertain (MW: perhaps = pṛṣṭha, ‘back’)
one that draws a cart (anas, ‘cart’ + √vah, ‘draw’): an ox

vyakarana.note: Nominative singular of paṣṭhavāh. MW records the nominative as -vāṭ in the Vājasaneyi and -vāt in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā; the text's paṣṭhavāc ca (t + c → cc) shows the t. Sāyaṇa's printed bhāṣya also writes the word with t (षष्ठवात्, with ṣ for p). The feminine is paṣṭhauhī, formed like dityauhī.
n-stem ukṣan, nominative singular ukṣā (the n is lost in the nominative).
A feminine consonant stem in t; the nominative is the bare stem, vehat, so vehac ca.
Nominative singular of anaḍuh, from the strong stem anaḍvāh- with n inserted in the nominative singular (P. 7.1.98, 7.1.82).

translation.literal: The four-year-old [male] and for me, the four-year-old [female] and for me, the bull (ukṣan) and for me, the barren cow and for me, the bull (ṛṣabha) and for me, the cow that miscarries and for me, the ox and for me, the milch cow and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May the bull and the heifer of four years be mine; the bull of breeding age and the barren cow; the older bull and the cow that has miscarried; the draught ox and the cow newly in milk.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the paṣṭhavāh is a bull of four years (चतुःसंवत्सर ऋषभः), and paṣṭhauhī a cow of that age («तथाविधा गौः पष्ठौही»). The ukṣan is the bull able to impregnate, «सेचनसमर्थ ऋषभ उक्षा»; the vaśā is a barren cow, «वन्ध्या गौर्वशा»; the ṛṣabha is a bull older even than the ukṣan, «उक्ष्णोऽप्याधिकवयस्क ऋषभः»; the vehat is a cow that loses her embryo (गर्भघातिनी); the anaḍvān is the bearer of a cart, «शकटस्य वाहकोऽनड्वान्»; and the dhenu is a cow that has newly calved, «नवप्रसूता गौर्धेनुः». In his comment on the eleventh anuvāka Sāyaṇa quotes the Brāhmaṇa on this first half of the tenth: it is the form of cattle, and by the form the sacrificer secures cattle.

flags.note: corrections.json C10.3-vehat: the base witness runs च and मे together after वेहत् and omits the svarita on च; the edition spaces them and restores the mark, as the second witness has it and as every other ‘X ca me’ of the Chamakam stands. The second witness also differs orthographically at म उक्षा (it leaves मे unchanged at a line end); the base witness's sandhi is kept.

Sāyaṇa distinguishes ukṣan (the bull able to breed) from ṛṣabha (a still older bull); the dictionaries give both simply as ‘bull’. For vehat MW gives ‘a barren cow or a cow that miscarries’; Sāyaṇa: गर्भघातिनी. The translation follows Sāyaṇa.
The first member of paṣṭhavāh is of uncertain sense; MW connects it, with a question mark, with pṛṣṭha ‘back’. Sāyaṇa states only the age (four years).

sandhi.rule: a visarga that stands for s, after a vowel other than a or ā, is r before a voiced sound (the s becomes r, sasajuṣo ruḥ, P. 8.2.66, and the r stays); so cakṣur yajñena
final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra, written as the nasal of the next consonant's class (P. 8.3.23, 8.4.59): m before p, ñ before c (kalpatāñ cakṣuḥ)
before m the nasal of the class is m itself: kalpatām manaḥ is written कल्पताम्मनो
-aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114); so apāno, vyāno, mano, yajño yajñena
final m before a vowel stays m and is joined to it in writing; so kalpatām ātmā
final m before y or v becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23), which the Taittirīya writes as the nasalised semivowel of the next word (P. 8.4.59): v̐ before vyānaḥ and vāk, y̐ before yajñaḥ and yajñena
final m before ś becomes anusvāra (written ँ in this text); śrotram before yajñena becomes śrotray̐ as above
a final stop is voiced before a voiced sound (jhalāṃ jaśo ’nte, P. 8.2.39): vāk becomes vāg before y

vyakarana.note: Imperative 3rd singular ātmanepada of kḷp (kalpate), ‘be fit, be in order, succeed’. This is the verb that, in Sāyaṇa's reading, is carried (anuṣaṅga) to every item of the Chamakam from the first anuvāka on; here it is stated, ten times.
Instrumental of means: ‘by, through the sacrifice’.
s-stem neuter āyus; nominative = the stem with s → ḥ. So cakṣuḥ, manaḥ.
Root noun vāc, f.; in pause the final c becomes k, voiced to g before yajñena.

translation.literal: May life be fit through the sacrifice; may the breath be fit through the sacrifice; may the down-breath be fit through the sacrifice; may the diffused breath be fit through the sacrifice; may the eye be fit through the sacrifice; may the ear be fit through the sacrifice; may the mind be fit through the sacrifice; may speech be fit through the sacrifice; may the self be fit through the sacrifice; may the sacrifice be fit through the sacrifice.
translation.readable: Through the sacrifice may life be made fit; through the sacrifice the breath, the down-breath and the diffused breath; through the sacrifice the eye and the ear, the mind and speech; through the sacrifice the self; and through the sacrifice may the sacrifice itself be made fit.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa treats life and the rest as well known («आयुरादयः प्रसिद्धाः») and glosses only ātman, as the body: «आत्मा शरीरम्». The prayer is that these become able to do their work by my sacrifice: «उक्ता आयुरादयो मदीयेन यज्ञेन कार्यक्षमा भवन्तु». The last yajñaḥ is a sacrifice still to be performed (करिष्यमाणः), such as the Aśvamedha (the printed text misprints the name), and it too is to become fit for its own work through the sacrifice now being performed: «सोऽप्यनेनानुष्ठीयमानेन यज्ञेन स्वकार्यक्षमो भवतु». In his comment on the eleventh anuvāka Sāyaṇa quotes the Brāhmaṇa, which calls these ten formulas kalpas and says they are offered so that what is not yet fit may become fit; in his comment on the first anuvāka he says that kalpatām, stated here, is to be supplied to every item of the Chamakam.
units.reflection: The last of the ten asks that the sacrifice be made fit by the sacrifice: the act is asked to set itself right as it is done.

flags.note: corrections.json C10.4-vyano and C10.4-yajno: two orthographic corrections to the base witness, both moving the anunāsika sign to the syllable where kalpatām meets the next word (कल्पताव्ँव्यानो, कल्पताय्ँयज्ञो), as the same witness writes it elsewhere in this unit. No letter of the words changes.
